templates.title: Pickup wait from check-in to handover, per store and hour of day
templates.subtopic: conditional aggregation over event pairs, GREATEST for a clock that starts late, local hour of day

sections.scenario: Grocery pickup customers reserve an hour-long slot, drive to the store and tap "I'm here" in the app; an associate brings the order out to the car. Store operations wants to see how long customers wait, per store and per hour of day, so it can staff the pickup area for the busy hours. Customers who arrive before their slot are early by their own choice, so this exercise's rule starts their wait at the slot start, not at the moment they checked in.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns store_id, hour_of_day, handovers, avg_wait_min, max_wait_min, over_target. For each order with a check-in and a handover, the wait starts at the later of its check-in and its slot_start, and the wait is the minutes from the wait start to the handover, never below 0 (a handover before the slot started is a wait of 0). hour_of_day is the hour (0–23) of the wait start. Group by store and hour of day: handovers counts the orders, avg_wait_min is the average wait rounded to 1 decimal place, max_wait_min the longest wait, and over_target counts waits longer than {{target}} minutes. Order by store_id, hour_of_day. {{event_rule}} {{tz_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Event times are recorded to the minute. The sample has {{orders}} orders; the result has one row per store and hour with at least one counted order.
sections.assumptions: Stores, slots, waits and the target are hypothetical; the wait rule is this exercise's rule, not any retailer's published standard. No customer or associate appears in the data: orders carry no customer identity, and nothing here measures an individual associate.
sections.criteria: One row per order with its first check-in and its handover; the wait starts at the later of check-in and slot start; waits clamped at 0; the hour of the wait start, in the store's local time at Very Hard; orders without both events left out; strict "over" the target; correct rounding and deterministic order; can discuss percentiles, invisible walk-ups and incremental builds.

clarifications.q: A customer checks in 20 minutes before the slot and gets the order 5 minutes after the slot starts. What is the wait?
clarifications.a: 5 minutes, measured from the slot start. That order counts in the hour of the slot start.

clarifications.q: Which hour does an on-time customer count in?
clarifications.a: The hour of the check-in, because that is when the wait started.

clarifications.q: Is a wait of exactly {{target}} minutes over the target?
clarifications.a: No. Only waits longer than the target count.

clarifications.q: How is the average rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 1) on the average of the per-order waits, half away from zero.

clarifications.q: What about an order that was never handed over?
clarifications.a: It has no wait and is left out, as is a handover with no check-in.

hints: Reduce the events to one row per order first: its check-in time and its handover time.
GREATEST(checkin_ts, slot_start) is the wait start; the wait is EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM handover_ts - wait_start) / 60, clamped at 0.
Take the hour of the wait start, not of the check-in. For a local hour, convert with AT TIME ZONE before extracting it.
followups: Operations asks for the 90th percentile wait instead of the average. What changes, and why can percentiles not be averaged across stores afterwards?
Some customers never tap "I'm here" and walk to the desk instead. How would you report how many handovers your metric cannot see, without guessing their waits?
A store moves its pickup area and its waits drop. How would you show the change fairly when the same week also had fewer orders in the busy hours?
At thousands of stores and millions of events a day, how would you build this incrementally, given that handovers arrive minutes to hours after check-ins?

rules.ask: A customer checks in at 10:40 for an 11:00 slot. Which hour does your query put that order in, and what does the specification say?
A customer taps "I'm here" twice. Which tap starts the wait, and why?
Is a wait of exactly the target over the target in your query?
A store in Los Angeles hands over an order at 8:30 pm local. Which UTC date and hour is that, and which hour does the report show?
Do you average the waits or the per-hour averages? Is there a difference when the hours have different numbers of orders?

templates.title: Substitutions rejected at handover, and short items with no substitute offered
templates.subtopic: latest row per group, anti-join, conditional counts, ISO weeks

sections.scenario: When an online grocery item is out of stock at the store picking the order, the picker can offer a substitute, which the customer accepts or rejects at handover. Two numbers tell the merchandising team whether substitutions are working: how often customers reject them, and how often an item was short with no substitute offered at all, a missed chance to keep the sale. They want both per product category and week.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns week_start, category, lines, substituted, rejected, reject_rate, short_no_offer, one row per week and category with at least one line in a completed order, ordered by week_start, category. week_start is the Monday of the UTC date of the order's pickup_ts; category is the category of the item the customer ordered (not of the substitute). lines counts the order lines. A line is substituted when it is short and has at least one row in sub_offers; it is rejected when the decision of its latest offer is rejected. reject_rate is rejected divided by substituted, rounded to 4 decimal places, and NULL when nothing was substituted. short_no_offer counts short lines with no offer whose customer allowed substitutes. {{offer_rule}} {{allow_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). (order_id, line_no) identifies a line. Offers for one line never share an offered_ts.
sections.assumptions: Categories, items, orders and decisions are hypothetical; the substitution rules (what counts as a substitution, how a missing response is read) are this exercise's rules, not any retailer's. Orders carry no customer identity; every figure is an aggregate.
sections.criteria: The latest offer per line with a deterministic tie-break; substitutions only on short lines; missed offers by anti-join, honouring allow_sub at Very Hard; cancelled orders left out at Hard+; the ordered item's category; Monday weeks from the UTC date; NULL rate when nothing was substituted and correct rounding; can discuss per-substitute rates, local dates, lost revenue and incremental builds.

clarifications.q: A milk line was substituted with oat milk from another category. Which category is it in?
clarifications.a: The ordered item's category. The question is how well each category's shortages are covered.

clarifications.q: Which week does an order picked up late on Sunday evening belong to?
clarifications.a: The week of its UTC date, starting on Monday, so Sunday belongs to the week that started six days earlier.

clarifications.q: Should a category-week with no substitutions show a rejection rate of 0?
clarifications.a: No. NULL: nothing was offered, so there is no rate.

clarifications.q: Does a short line with no offer count as substituted?
clarifications.a: No. It is counted in short_no_offer instead (when the customer allowed substitutes).

clarifications.q: How is the rate rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(rejected::numeric / substituted, 4), half away from zero.

hints: Pick each line's latest offer first: DISTINCT ON (order_id, line_no) … ORDER BY order_id, line_no, offered_ts DESC, offer_id DESC, or ROW_NUMBER().
LEFT JOIN that to the lines of completed orders; a short line with no latest offer is a missed offer.
date_trunc('week', …) starts weeks on Monday. NULLIF(substituted, 0) gives the NULL rate.
followups: The team wants a rejection rate per substitute item as well, to stop offering bad substitutes. What is the grain now, and what is the denominator?
Customers can also reject at handover in the store's local evening, while the week here is UTC. Which orders change weeks if you use each store's local date, and does that matter for a weekly trend?
Rejected substitutions are refunded and missed offers lose the sale. How would you turn both numbers into lost revenue, and which prices would you use?
At hundreds of millions of lines a month, offers keep arriving until handover. How would you build this incrementally without recounting closed weeks?

rules.ask: The picker offered one substitute, the customer rejected it, and a second was accepted. Which decision does your query use, and why?
Which category does a substituted line count in, and what would change if it were the substitute's?
What does a NULL decision mean here, and how did you count it?
Does your join drop short lines that had no offer? Where do they show up in the result?
What is the denominator of reject_rate, and why not every short line?

templates.title: Phantom inventory suspects: stock on hand, but no sales for three days
templates.subtopic: date spines, netting per day, windows counted in open days, NOT EXISTS

sections.scenario: A store's system can say it has an item on hand while the shelf is empty: the units were miscounted, damaged or misplaced. Customers cannot buy what is not there, and replenishment does not reorder what it believes is on hand, so the item quietly stops selling. A useful first signal is an item that normally sells every day, still shows stock, and has not sold for three days. Store teams then check the shelf and correct the count.
sections.problem: As of {{as_of}}, write one PostgreSQL query that lists the store-items that are phantom inventory suspects under this exercise's rule, returning store_id, item_id, baseline_days_sold, baseline_units, on_hand, ordered by store_id, item_id. For each store, the check window is its last 3 days up to and including the as-of date, and the baseline is the {{baseline_days}} days immediately before the check window. A day sold when the item's net units that day (the sum of its sales rows) is above 0. A store-item is a suspect when all three hold: its end-of-day on_hand is above 0 on each of the 3 check days; it sold on none of the check days; and it sold on at least {{min_days}} of the {{baseline_days}} baseline days. baseline_days_sold counts those baseline days, baseline_units sums its net units over the baseline days, and on_hand is the snapshot on the last day of the check window. {{sales_rule}} {{closure_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). sales covers every day from {{first_day}} to the as-of date: a day with no row has 0 units. inventory_snapshots holds end-of-day counts for the last 7 days. Every store-item in sales is in scope.
sections.assumptions: Stores, items, units and thresholds are hypothetical. The suspect rule is this exercise's rule; real out-of-stock detection uses more signals (expected sales rates, deliveries, cycle counts). The output is a list of store-items to check, never a statement about any associate.
sections.criteria: Windows defined as the last 3 and the preceding {{baseline_days}} days per store, counted in open days at Very Hard; sales netted per day and only a positive net counted as sold; stock positive on every check day, with a missing snapshot not positive; the inclusive threshold; days with no row treated as 0 units; correct outputs and order; can discuss probabilistic rules, deliveries, measuring precision and incremental computation.

clarifications.q: A day has no sales row for the item. Is that a day without a sale?
clarifications.a: Yes. No row means 0 units.

clarifications.q: The item sold on exactly {{min_days}} baseline days. Is that enough?
clarifications.a: Yes. "At least" includes the threshold.

clarifications.q: What if the snapshot shows 0 on one of the check days?
clarifications.a: Then the shelf really was empty that day (it sold out); the store-item is not a suspect.

clarifications.q: Is the as-of date itself in the check window?
clarifications.a: Yes. The check window ends on the as-of date (or, when stores close, on its last open day).

clarifications.q: Does a day with a return count as a sale?
clarifications.a: No. Only a day whose net units are above 0 sold.

hints: Build a spine of days per store (generate_series), and number them backwards from the as-of date with ROW_NUMBER(): numbers 1–3 are the check window, the next {{baseline_days}} the baseline.
Net the sales per store, item and day before deciding whether a day sold.
Count check days with a positive snapshot (a missing snapshot is not positive) and require all three; bool_and or a count of 3 both work.
followups: Fast sellers can go three days without a sale by chance less often than slow ones. How would you replace the fixed "sold on at least {{min_days}} days" rule with a probability based on each item's daily sales rate?
A delivery arrived during the check window and the item still did not sell. Is that stronger or weaker evidence, and how would you use it?
After store teams correct the count, how would you measure whether the suspect list is precise enough to be worth their time?
At thousands of stores and hundreds of thousands of items, how would you compute this daily without scanning a month of sales each night?

rules.ask: A store was closed on one of the last three days. Does your window count it, and should it?
A day has a sale and a return of the same units. Does your query count it as a sold day?
A snapshot is missing for one check day. What does your query assume the stock was?
An item sold on exactly {{min_days}} baseline days. Is it a suspect under your query?
Does your window frame count rows or days? What happens on a day with no sales row?

templates.title: Sales over any time range while voids and late register uploads keep correcting the past
templates.subtopic: point updates and range sums, transaction state for voids and corrections

sections.scenario: A store's sales dashboard answers questions such as "what did we sell between 2:15 and 3:40 last Tuesday?" over any range of minutes. The data is never final: registers that were offline upload their transactions late, into minutes already reported; voids cancel transactions that were already counted; and a register whose clock was wrong sends a correction that moves a transaction to its true minute. The dashboard must answer each question from the data as it stands at that moment.
sections.problem:
Implement range_sales(n_minutes, ops). Minutes are numbered 0 … n_minutes − 1. ops is processed in order; each is one of:

  • ('sale', txn_id, minute, cents): a transaction of cents (a positive integer) at minute. Every sale's txn_id is unique.
  • ('void', txn_id): the transaction no longer counts.
  • ('move', txn_id, minute): the transaction's true minute is minute.
  • ('query', lo, hi): the total cents of the counted transactions whose minute is in lo … hi, inclusive. lo and hi are valid minutes; when lo > hi the range is empty and the answer is 0.

Return the list of query answers, in order. {{void_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to about a year of minutes (n_minutes up to 600 000), 150 000 sales with their voids and moves, and 30 000 queries whose ranges can span months, interleaved. Expected: O((u + q) log n) for u updates and q queries. Re-adding every minute of a range for each query is too slow, and so is rebuilding prefix sums after every update.
sections.assumptions: Registers, transactions and amounts are hypothetical. Amounts are integer cents; taxes, tenders and returns are out of scope. The operations arrive in one ordered stream.
sections.criteria: A dict of transaction state plus a Fenwick (or segment) tree over minutes; inclusive ranges and 0 for lo > hi; voids and moves applied only to transactions that still count; repeated voids harmless; at Very Hard, voids that arrive before their sale and moves of unknown transactions handled as specified; O((u + q) log n); can discuss window maxima, more dimensions and read/write trade-offs.

clarifications.q: A sale is uploaded late into a minute that an earlier query already covered. Does that earlier answer change?
clarifications.a: No. Each query is answered from the data as it stands when it arrives; later queries see the late sale.

clarifications.q: Is the range inclusive at both ends?
clarifications.a: Yes. ('query', 5, 5) is the single minute 5.

clarifications.q: What does a query with lo > hi return?
clarifications.a: 0, an empty range. It is not an error.

clarifications.q: Can a void be undone?
clarifications.a: No. Once voided, a transaction never counts again, even if it is moved.

clarifications.q: Can I keep a list of totals per minute and add up the range?
clarifications.a: That is correct but O(range) per query; with ranges of months and tens of thousands of queries it is too slow.

hints: Separate two concerns: a dict from txn_id to its minute, amount and whether it still counts; and a structure over minutes that supports "add to one minute" and "total of a range".
A range total is prefix(hi + 1) − prefix(lo). A Fenwick tree gives both prefix totals and point updates in O(log n).
A void subtracts the amount at its current minute; a move subtracts at the old minute and adds at the new one, but only while the transaction still counts.
followups: Store managers also want the busiest 15-minute window in any range. What would you add to the structure, and what does an update cost then?
The dashboard needs totals per store and per department over any range. How does the structure grow, and when would you switch to a two-dimensional Fenwick tree or to pre-aggregated blocks?
Queries arrive at a few per second and updates at thousands per second. Which side would you make cheaper, and how?
In a warehouse, the same corrections arrive as files hours later. How would you keep minute totals correct and auditable there, and what do you lose compared with this in-memory structure?

rules.ask: A query spans three months of minutes and there are 30,000 of them. How many additions does your loop do in total?
Every query follows an update in this stream. How often do you rebuild the prefix sums, and what does each rebuild cost?
A segment tree works here too. What would make you choose it over a Fenwick tree, and what does it cost in memory?
A transaction is voided and then moved. What happens to the totals in your code?
What is the cost per query and per update with your blocks, and how did you choose the block size?

templates.title: Expiring stock: units of each delivered lot that expire unsold
templates.subtopic: FIFO consumption per key with expiry, amortised analysis

sections.scenario: Fresh items arrive at a store in lots, each with its own expiry date. Under this exercise's rule, every sale takes units from the oldest lot of the item on the shelf, first in, first out. Units still on the shelf after their lot's expiry date are thrown away. The fresh team wants to know, lot by lot, how many units expired unsold, to tune order sizes and delivery days.
sections.problem:
Implement expired_units(lots, sales, writeoffs, as_of).

  • lots: (lot_id, item, delivered_day, units, expiry_day), sorted by delivered_day; delivered_day ≤ expiry_day.
  • sales: (day, item, units), sorted by day.
  • writeoffs: (day, lot_id, units), sorted by day.

Days are integers, and every sale and write-off is on a day ≤ as_of. On each day, the lots delivered that day arrive first, then the write-offs of that day apply, then the sales of that day happen in list order. A sale on day d takes units from the oldest lot of its item that has been delivered (delivered_day ≤ d), has not expired (expiry_day ≥ d) and has units left; the oldest is the earliest delivered_day, then the earlier position in lots. When that lot runs out the sale continues from the next oldest; units that no lot can supply are lost (not owed later). A lot's units still left at the end of its expiry_day expire. Return {lot_id: expired units} for every lot whose expiry_day < as_of (including lots with 0 expired units); lots that have not expired by as_of are left out. {{item_rule}} {{writeoff_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 50 000 lots and 150 000 sales over thousands of days, across several items. Expected: O(n + L) after the inputs, for n sales and L lots (plus the write-offs). Scanning the lots from the oldest on every sale is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Items, lots, units and shelf lives are hypothetical, and selling oldest-first is this exercise's rule; real stores rotate stock by hand and customers pick from the front or the back. Markdowns and transfers are out of scope.
sections.criteria: A queue of lots per item with sold-out and expired lots removed from the front for good; oldest-first across lots, including a newer lot that expires first; sellable through the expiry day; lost units not carried forward; correct inclusion rule for as_of; at Very Hard, write-offs by lot id, capped at what is left, ignored after expiry, before the day's sales; O(n + L) with an amortised argument; can discuss first-expiring-first-out and replaying alternative plans.

clarifications.q: Can a lot be sold on its expiry day?
clarifications.a: Yes. It is sellable through expiry_day and expires at the end of that day.

clarifications.q: The oldest lot expires after a newer lot. Which one sells first?
clarifications.a: The oldest, always; the rule is first in, first out, not first expiring.

clarifications.q: A sale wants 10 units and only 6 are on the shelf. What happens to the other 4?
clarifications.a: They are lost. Later deliveries do not fill them.

clarifications.q: Is a lot with expiry_day == as_of in the result?
clarifications.a: No. It can still be sold on as_of, so it has not expired yet.

clarifications.q: Are lots with nothing expired in the result?
clarifications.a: Yes, with 0, as long as their expiry_day < as_of.

hints: Keep a queue of lot ids per item. Deliveries go on the back; a sale looks only at the front.
A lot at the front that is sold out, or whose expiry_day is before today, can be removed for good: days only move forward, so it can never be sold again.
Once a lot is past its expiry day nothing touches it any more, so its units left at the end are exactly its expired units.
followups: Change the rule to first expiring, first out (the lot with the earliest expiry_day sells first). Which data structure replaces the queue, and what does a sale cost now?
Explain why your solution is O(n + L) even though a single sale can walk through many lots.
The team wants to try "order 20% less on days before a slow day". How would you replay a year of sales with a different delivery plan, and what would you hold fixed?
Expiry is per lot, but stores record sales per item, not per lot. What do you lose by inferring lots with this rule, and how would you check it against counted waste?

rules.ask: A shelf has 10,000 lots behind it by the end of the year. How many lots does each sale look at in your code?
What does pop(0) cost on a Python list, and what would you use instead?
Which order does your heap use, and is that the rule here, oldest delivered or earliest expiry?
A sale happens on a lot's expiry day. Does your code sell from that lot?
A write-off arrives the day after the lot expired. What does it change in your code, and what should it change?

templates.title: Frequently bought together: item pairs that share at least s baskets
templates.subtopic: pair co-occurrence per basket, support thresholds, ordering

sections.scenario: A merchandising team wants to know which items customers buy together, so that it can place them near each other in stores and suggest one when the other is in an online cart. A basket is one register transaction or one online order, reduced to the list of items in it. A pair of items counts as "frequently bought together" when it appears in at least s baskets, the pair's support. The first version of the report is a plain count, before any lift or confidence measure is added.
sections.problem: Implement frequent_pairs(baskets, s, max_items=None). baskets is a list of baskets, and each basket is a list of item names. A pair (a, b) is two different items with a < b, and it appears in a basket if both items do. A basket counts once for a pair, however many times either item is listed in it. Return a list of (a, b, count) for every pair that appears in at least s baskets, where count is the number of baskets it appears in. Order the list by count descending, then by a, then by b. If no pair qualifies, return an empty list. {{basket_rule}} {{bulk_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 50 000 baskets over a catalogue of 5 000 items, with at most about ten distinct items in an ordinary basket. s is at least 1. Item names are plain ASCII names or codes, compared as Python strings. Something close to O(Σ b²) is expected, where b is the number of distinct items in each basket that is counted. Checking every pair of catalogue items against every basket, O(I²·n), is far too slow, and so is intersecting per-item sets of baskets for every pair of items.
sections.assumptions: Baskets, item names and thresholds are hypothetical. The bulk-basket rule is this exercise's rule; check current docs for any real product. Quantities do not matter: buying six cans of one soup is the same as buying one for this report.
sections.criteria: Each basket counted once per pair, with repeats removed first; no item paired with itself; pairs in name order; the support threshold inclusive at exactly s; the stated ordering with tie-breaks; empty and one-item baskets handled; bulk baskets skipped by distinct-item count before pairs are generated; counting inside each basket, with a clear O(Σ b²) argument and why the set-intersection approach does not scale; sensible answers on lift, distributed counting and triples.

clarifications.q: If milk appears twice in a basket with bread, is that two baskets for (bread, milk)?
clarifications.a: No. A basket counts once for a pair, however many times its items are listed.

clarifications.q: Is an item paired with itself when it is listed twice?
clarifications.a: No. A pair is two different items.

clarifications.q: Which way round is a pair written?
clarifications.a: Name order: a < b as Python compares strings, whatever order the items were scanned in.

clarifications.q: How are ties in count ordered?
clarifications.a: By a, then by b, both ascending. The output is fully determined.

clarifications.q: When max_items is set, do repeated items count towards it?
clarifications.a: No. It limits distinct items: a basket with the same three items listed twice has three.

hints: How many pairs does one basket of b distinct items contain? Add that up over the baskets. That is the work you cannot avoid, and it is small.
Turn each basket into a sorted set of distinct items first. Then every pair comes out already in name order.
Check max_items before you generate any pair from a basket. A basket of 4 000 items holds about eight million pairs.
followups: Bananas and milk appear in a large share of all baskets, so they top the list with everything. What measure would you report instead of the raw count, and what does it do to rare items?
The pair counts must cover a year of baskets across every store. How do you compute them in a distributed job, and where does the shuffle get large?
The team now wants triples. How does the work grow, and how would the pair results let you prune the candidates?
A pair's support jumps for one week in one region. How would you tell a real change in what customers buy from a promotion, a planogram change or a data problem?

rules.ask: How many pairs does combinations produce for a basket of 4 000 items, and where in your loop do you make sure that never happens?
Pruning items with support below s first is a good idea. At these sizes most items pass it. What does the pair step cost after pruning?
Intersecting two items' basket sets is fast. How many intersections does it take for 5 000 items, and how large is each one?
How many distinct pairs can your dictionary end up holding over a year of baskets, and what would you do when it no longer fits in memory?
Write the formula. What happens to lift for a pair of items that each appear in only three baskets?

templates.title: Store floor heat map: sales over many rectangular floor areas
templates.subtopic: 2D prefix sums, inclusion-exclusion, clipping rectangles

sections.scenario: A store's sales floor is divided into a grid of equal cells, and each cell holds the week's net sales, in whole dollars, of the items displayed there. Store planners draw rectangles on a floor plan (an end cap, an aisle block, a seasonal area, a department) and want the total sales inside each one. A planning tool sends tens of thousands of rectangles at once, for many layouts it compares, so each answer must be cheap.
sections.problem: Implement area_sales(grid, queries). grid[r][c] is the net sales of the cell in row r and column c. Every row has the same length, and the grid has at least one cell. Each query (r1, c1, r2, c2) names two opposite corner cells of a rectangle, and both corners are inside it. Return a list with the total of the cells inside each rectangle, in query order. {{corner_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 600 rows by 800 columns and 80 000 rectangles, many of them covering most of the floor. Values are integers with an absolute value below 10 000. Something close to O(R·C + q) is expected. Summing each rectangle, even row by row with slices, is too slow, and so is a prefix sum per row that still loops over the rows of every rectangle.
sections.assumptions: Floor layouts and sales are hypothetical. How sales are credited to a cell, and how returns are credited back, is this exercise's rule. The grid does not change while one batch of rectangles is answered.
sections.criteria: A 2D prefix-sum table with an extra row and column, built in one pass; correct inclusion-exclusion with inclusive corners; corners put in order where they can come either way; rectangles clipped to the floor and empty ones returning 0; negative cells handled; O(R·C + q) explained, and why per-rectangle summing (even with C-speed slices or per-row prefixes) does not scale; credible answers on updates, the best fixed-size area and storage across stores.

clarifications.q: Are both corners included?
clarifications.a: Yes. (2, 3, 2, 3) is the single cell in row 2, column 3.

clarifications.q: Can I assume r1 <= r2 and c1 <= c2?
clarifications.a: Only where the rules above say so. Read them for this replay.

clarifications.q: Can a total be negative?
clarifications.a: Yes, when cells with returns outweigh the rest.

clarifications.q: What if a rectangle has no cell on the floor?
clarifications.a: Where rectangles can leave the floor, a rectangle with no cell on it totals 0.

clarifications.q: May I use NumPy?
clarifications.a: Answer in plain Python first. Then say what NumPy would and would not change about the complexity.

hints: Let P[i][j] be the total of every cell above and to the left of (i, j), exclusive. One pass over the grid fills it.
A rectangle's total is four lookups in P: the large corner, minus the strip above, minus the strip to the left, plus the corner you subtracted twice.
Put the corners in order and clip them to the floor before you look anything up. An empty range after clipping means 0.
followups: Sales update every hour, one cell at a time, while planners keep querying. What structure keeps both updates and queries fast, and what does each cost?
Planners now want the busiest 3 × 4 area on the floor, anywhere. How do you find it, and how fast?
The heat map should cover every store in the chain, each with its own floor size, every week for two years. How would you store the prefix sums, and what would you precompute?
Cells are not equal in practice: a freezer aisle and a clothing rack have very different sales per square foot. How would you make the heat map fair to compare across areas?

rules.ask: A row slice is summed at C speed. How many slices does one tall rectangle take, and how many slices is that for 80 000 rectangles?
With a prefix sum per row, what does one rectangle still cost, and how would you remove the loop over its rows?
NumPy makes each rectangle's sum fast. What is the total work across all rectangles, and what precomputation would make each one O(1) in NumPy too?
That supports updates. What does a query cost in two dimensions, and when is a plain prefix-sum table better?
Show your four lookups for a rectangle that starts at row 0. How does your table avoid an index of -1?

templates.title: Debug the store replenishment order calculator
templates.subtopic: rounding to case packs, stock positions, time zones, renamed fields

sections.scenario: Every night a calculator decides how many cases of each item each store should order, so that the shelf covers the forecast for the next few days plus some safety stock. Store teams have raised several complaints. Shelves run out a day early, because orders arrive one case short. Stores with full backrooms keep receiving more of the same item. A store whose count went negative after a late receipt over-ordered. Items already delivered are treated as if they were still on the way. Stores in the west order for the wrong days. The function below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix replenishment_orders(positions, forecast, stores, start, end) so that it meets this specification. stores maps each store to its offset from UTC in whole hours. start and end are store-local dates, YYYY-MM-DD, inclusive. {{replay_rule}}

  1. Forecast. Each row {"store", "item", "utc", "units"} is the units expected to sell in the hour that starts at utc, a UTC timestamp written YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM without a zone. It counts towards the item's need at that store if the store-local date of that hour (UTC plus the store's offset) is between start and end. Rows for a store and item with no position are ignored.
  2. Available stock. Each position {"store", "item", "on_hand", "backroom", "case_pack", "safety", "open_orders"} has available stock max(on_hand, 0) + backroom + units on order. on_hand is the sales-floor count, and it can be negative when sales are scanned before a receipt is recorded; this exercise treats a negative count as 0. Units on order are cases × case_pack summed over open_orders whose status is "open". A "received" order is already in the counts, and a "cancelled" order will not arrive.
  3. Order. The shortfall is need + safety − available. If it is positive, the store orders the smallest whole number of cases that covers it. Otherwise it orders nothing.
  4. Output. A dict {"<store>/<item>": cases} with an entry only for positions that order at least one case.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 40 000 positions and 200 000 forecast rows, processed in linear time. Offsets are fixed for the window (this exercise's simplification: no daylight-saving change inside it).
sections.assumptions: Stores, items, forecasts and the ordering rule are hypothetical and simplified; they are this exercise's rules, not any retailer's. Lead times, minimum orders and shelf capacity are left out.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with the complaint it caused; whole-case rounding up; backroom stock read from the right field; a negative on-hand treated as 0 without hiding backroom or open orders; only open orders counted as still to come; forecast hours bucketed by store-local date with each store's own offset; minimal, linear fixes; a test per bug.

clarifications.q: Is a negative on-hand an error?
clarifications.a: It is a count that is behind reality. The order uses 0 for it, and the negative number is a signal for a cycle count, outside this function.

clarifications.q: Does backroom stock count, even though it is not on the shelf?
clarifications.a: Yes. It can be moved to the shelf without an order.

clarifications.q: Which date does a forecast hour belong to?
clarifications.a: The store-local date of the hour's start: UTC plus the store's offset, which is negative for stores west of UTC.

clarifications.q: Can a store order part of a case?
clarifications.a: No. It orders whole cases, enough to cover the whole shortfall.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Work one position by hand: 10 on hand, safety 4, a forecast of 20, a case pack of 6. How many cases does the code order, and how many cover the shortfall?
Print the keys of a position dict, and compare them with every key the code reads.
Take a store at UTC−5 and a forecast hour at 02:00 UTC on the first day of the window. Which local date is that?
List the statuses an open order can have, and which of them add stock that is not yet counted.
followups: The forecast is uncertain, and some items sell in bursts. How would you set safety stock per item and store, and what data would you use?
A case pack changes from 6 to 12 in the middle of the week, while orders in the old pack are still open. What breaks, and how would you store pack sizes?
Some stores show negative on-hand counts every week for the same items. What does that tell you, and how would you turn it into a list of counts to do?
This runs nightly for thousands of stores across six time zones. When does each store's run start, and how do you handle a forecast or a receipt that arrives late?

rules.ask: Your ceiling divides with /, which gives a float. Up to what size is that exact, and what integer-only form avoids the question?
The order treats a negative count as 0. Who should still see the negative number, and what would they do with it?
This exercise fixes offsets for the window. What changes when the window crosses a daylight-saving change, and where would the store's zone name come from?
A receipt is recorded a day after the truck arrived. For that day, is the order counted twice, not at all, or once? What would you check?

templates.title: Weighted and variable-price grocery items, from estimated to final charge
templates.subtopic: order line lifecycle, estimates versus actuals, money in minor units, reconciliation

sections.scenario: An online grocery service takes about {{daily_orders}} pickup and delivery orders a day, picked in {{stores}} stores. About {{weighted_share}} of order lines are sold by weight or have a variable price: loose produce, deli counter items, and packaged meat whose price depends on the weight of the pack. When the customer orders, the line shows an estimated price based on an average weight, and the payment method is authorised for the estimated total plus a buffer of {{hold_buffer}} (this exercise's rule; check current docs). At picking, the associate records the actual weight or the price on the pack. Some lines are substituted, some are short, and some are returned afterwards. The customer pays the final amount, which can differ from the estimate.
sections.problem: Design the data model and pipeline that carries each line from the estimate to the final charge and beyond. Cover the events and their keys (order placed, line edited, picked with weight or price, substituted, short, handed over, returned), how the final charge per line is computed and rounded, what happens when the final total exceeds the authorised amount, how refunds for returns are calculated for weighed items, and the analytics on top: estimate accuracy per item and store, the share of orders that exceed the buffer, and the difference between estimated and final revenue per day.
sections.constraints: Money is stored as integer cents and weight as integer grams (or thousandths of a pound). The line's final price is computed and rounded once (this exercise's rule: half up to the cent). Events from store devices can arrive late or twice. A customer's receipt must be reproducible exactly, months later. Store and customer data appear in reports only in aggregate.
sections.assumptions: Order volumes, shares, buffers and rounding rules are hypothetical, and they are this exercise's rules, not a description of any retailer's checkout or payment flow. Each picked weighed line carries a measured weight from a scale, or a printed price and weight from a pre-packed label.
sections.criteria: Estimate and actual kept as separate facts; an event model keyed by order line and fulfilment step, with deduplication; final charges computed from recorded inputs with one stated rounding rule in integer cents; the over-buffer case designed end to end; substitutions, shorts and partial returns linked to the original line; receipts reproducible from stored inputs and rule versions; analytics in aggregate for merchandising, operations and finance; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Is the estimate per unit or per line?
clarifications.a: Per line: the ordered quantity times an average weight times the price per kilogram or pound, or an average pack price for variable-price packs.

clarifications.q: What if the final total exceeds the authorised amount?
clarifications.a: That is one of the cases you must design for. Say what the system does and what the customer sees.

clarifications.q: Can the price per kilogram change between the order and the pick?
clarifications.a: Yes. You decide which price applies, state it as this exercise's rule, and record both.

clarifications.q: How is a substitute for a weighed item priced?
clarifications.a: Choose a rule and state it; the data model must record the original line, the substitute and the price rule used.

clarifications.q: Who reads the analytics?
clarifications.a: Merchandising (estimate accuracy per item), store operations (picking and weighing) and finance (estimated versus captured revenue).

hints: Keep the estimate and the actual as two separate facts on the line, never one field that is overwritten.
Compute the final charge per line from the recorded inputs (weight, unit price, rule version), so a receipt can be rebuilt exactly.
Separate the order line from its fulfilment: one ordered line can become a substitute, a partial pick and a return.
followups: A scale in one store was mis-calibrated for a week. How do you find the affected lines, and what do you do about the charges?
The final total exceeds the authorised amount for 2% of orders on a holiday. What options exist, and what data would you use to choose the buffer?
A customer returns half of a weighed item. How is the refund calculated, and what does the line look like afterwards?
Estimates for one item are systematically 20% low in one region. How would you detect it, and who changes the average weight?

rules.ask: Which amounts and weights do you store as what type, and where exactly does rounding happen?
The estimate was overwritten by the actual. How do you now measure estimate accuracy, or rebuild the receipt the customer saw at checkout?
The final total is above the authorised amount. Walk through what happens to the order and what the customer is told.
The substitute is sold by the pack, not by weight. Which price is charged, and where is that rule recorded?

incidents: About {{weighted_share}} of lines are weighed. After a price-file update, one store's deli prices per kilogram are ten times too high for three hours, and those orders are handed over before anyone notices.
On a holiday peak, 3% of orders exceed the {{hold_buffer}} buffer, and the pipeline's daily revenue report shows captured revenue above the authorised total.
A store device loses connectivity and sends the morning's pick events, with weights, twice after reconnecting.

templates.title: Register transactions into analytics, reconciled to the tills
templates.subtopic: store-and-forward ingestion, voids and returns, late data, daily reconciliation

sections.scenario: A retailer runs {{stores}} stores with about {{registers}} registers each, including self-checkout, and records about {{daily_transactions}} register transactions a day. Registers keep selling when the store loses its connection, and forward their transactions later; a register can be offline for up to {{offline_hours}}. A transaction can be voided before it completes, a line can be voided inside a transaction, and returns can be made at any store for purchases made elsewhere or online. Every evening each store closes its tills, and finance treats the till totals as the truth. Analytics must show daily sales by store, department and item that agree with the tills.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from the registers to daily sales tables. Cover the transaction record and its identity, how registers forward their transactions and what makes a resend harmless, how voids, line voids and returns are represented, which business date a transaction belongs to (store-local date, transactions that cross midnight, registers with a wrong clock), how late transactions update days already published, how you reconcile your daily totals with the till close and what happens when they disagree, and the tables analysts use.
sections.constraints: A transaction must be counted exactly once, however many times it is sent. A day's sales may change after publication, and every change must be explainable. Reconciliation with the tills must run per store and day, and a difference must name the registers and transactions behind it. Customer data stays out of these tables; reports are by store, department and item.
sections.assumptions: Store counts, volumes and offline durations are hypothetical. Each register numbers its transactions in sequence and stamps them with its own clock. The till close produces totals per register and tender type. Business-date and return rules are this exercise's rules.
sections.criteria: A register-generated transaction identity and deduplication on it; sequence gaps used to measure completeness; voids, line voids and returns modelled explicitly and linked; a clear business-date rule in store-local time with clock problems detected; late data applied as versioned, explainable corrections to published days; per-store, per-register reconciliation with the till close that names the transactions behind a difference; analyst tables by store, department and item, with no customer data; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Which date does a return belong to?
clarifications.a: The date and store where the return happens. It is linked to the original sale when the receipt is known.

clarifications.q: Is a voided transaction sent at all?
clarifications.a: Yes, with a void status. A line void appears as a line with a negative quantity, linked to the line it cancels.

clarifications.q: How late can a transaction arrive?
clarifications.a: Typically minutes, but up to {{offline_hours}} when a store is offline, and occasionally days after a register is repaired.

clarifications.q: Does the register clock always agree with the store's?
clarifications.a: No. Some registers drift or are set to the wrong zone after a repair.

clarifications.q: Is the till close always right?
clarifications.a: Finance treats it as the record. When analytics disagrees, you must show why, not quietly adjust either side.

hints: Give every transaction an identity that the register itself creates, such as store, register and sequence number, and use it to make resends harmless.
Gaps in a register's sequence numbers tell you exactly which transactions are still missing.
Treat a published day as a version. A late transaction creates a new version of that day, with the difference recorded.
followups: A store was offline for {{offline_hours}} on its busiest day. Walk through what each table shows during the outage, after reconnection, and after the till close.
A register's clock was set to the wrong year after a repair, and it sold for a day. How do you detect it, and which date do its transactions get?
Finance's till total for one store and day is 0.4% higher than yours. How do you find the cause, and who signs off?
Item-level sales feed replenishment and price analytics within the hour. How do you serve them fast while still reconciling to the tills at night?

rules.ask: Some register clocks are wrong. Which time decides the business date, and how do you notice a clock that has drifted?
What is the key you deduplicate on, how long do you keep it, and what happens to a transaction resent after that?
A transaction from three days ago arrives. How does the day's total change, and how do you show analysts what changed?
An upsert replaces a row. How do you still explain to finance why yesterday's total moved after it was published?
A register restarts and its sequence begins again at 1. How does your gap detection tell that from missing transactions?

incidents: A region loses connectivity for {{offline_hours}} on a Saturday; when stores reconnect, their registers forward the backlog together, and several also resend transactions they had already sent.
One register's clock is set to the wrong time zone after a repair, and for two days its sales land on the wrong business date.
Analytics totals for 30 of {{stores}} stores are below the till close after a register software update changed how line voids are sent.

templates.title: Items and prices across channels — store, online and marketplace offers, rollbacks, clearance and the price shown on a date
templates.subtopic: effective-dated prices, precedence of price types, zones and store exceptions, bitemporal corrections

sections.scenario: A retailer sells in {{stores}} stores and online. Its online catalogue holds about {{online_items}} items, most of them offered by marketplace sellers rather than by the retailer itself. In this exercise store prices are set per price zone ({{price_zones}} zones), with exceptions for individual stores; the retailer's own online price can differ from any store's; and each marketplace seller sets its own price for its own offer. A price can be regular, a rollback (a temporary lower price with a start and an end), clearance (a permanent markdown on an item being sold through), or online-only. There are about {{weekly_changes}} price changes a week. Merchants, the website and customer care all ask the same question in different words: what price did item X carry at store S, or online, on date D, and which rule produced it?
sections.problem: Design the data model for items, offers and prices across the three channels. Cover the item and its variants; an offer per channel (a store item, the retailer's online offer, each seller's marketplace offer); prices as effective-dated records with a type; zones, zone membership over time and store exceptions; the precedence that resolves several applicable prices into one price of record; and a derived table that answers "the price on a date" quickly. Show how a price recorded late, or recorded wrongly and corrected, is kept, so that you can answer both "what was true on D" and "what did we believe on D".
sections.constraints: Money is stored in integer cents. In this exercise's rule the precedence is clearance, then rollback, then regular, with a store exception beating its zone's price of the same type; an item on clearance in a store is never put on rollback there. Store prices take effect at the start of the store's local day; the online price takes effect at a stated instant. A store's zone can change, and history must keep the zone the store was in at the time. Nothing is ever overwritten: a correction is a new record. Marketplace prices belong to their sellers and are kept apart from the retailer's own prices.
sections.assumptions: Store counts, zone counts, catalogue size and change volume are hypothetical. Price-matching at the register, coupons and loyalty discounts are out of scope. Tax is out of scope.
sections.criteria: Items, offers per channel and prices as typed, effective-dated records, never overwritten; zone membership effective-dated; a stated precedence with store exceptions and clearance over rollback; the "was" price derivable; a second time axis for corrections and late records; a resolved price-of-record table with a sound refresh strategy; store-local effective times; marketplace prices kept per seller; the incidents explained by the model and fixed without rewriting history.

clarifications.q: Is the price shown on the shelf the same as the price charged at the register?
clarifications.a: They should be equal; in this exercise the register applies the price of record. If they disagree, the register's charged price is the evidence for what the customer paid.

clarifications.q: Does a rollback carry a "was" price?
clarifications.a: Yes. In this exercise the shelf and the page show the regular price the rollback replaces, so the model must be able to produce it for that date.

clarifications.q: Can two rollbacks for one item overlap in one zone?
clarifications.a: Not by rule, but the input sometimes contains them. Say what your model does with an overlap.

clarifications.q: Does the online price follow a store?
clarifications.a: No. The retailer's online price is national here, but pickup orders are charged the price of the pickup store in this exercise.

clarifications.q: How far back must "the price on a date" go?
clarifications.a: Three years for merchants and customer care.

hints: Separate what was decided (price records with a type, scope, valid-from and valid-to) from what was resolved (the price of record per offer and day).
Two time axes: when a price is in force, and when the system learned of it. A late record and a correction differ only in the second.
A zone is a group of stores whose membership changes; keep membership as its own effective-dated table.
followups: Write the resolution rule as a query or pseudocode: for one store, one item and one date, which records apply and which wins?
A rollback in one zone starts on Friday. On Wednesday the merchant shortens it by two days. What rows exist afterwards, and what does "what did we believe on Thursday" return?
Thirty stores move from one zone to another on the first of the month. Which rows change, and what does last month's price history for those stores show?

With {{weekly_changes}} changes a week across {{price_zones}} zones, would you materialise the resolved price per store, item and day, or per zone with store exceptions? Estimate the row counts and say how you keep it current.
A marketplace seller and the retailer both offer the same item online. Customer care asks what the customer saw. Which tables answer it, and what do you need to have logged at the time?

rules.ask: A rollback was entered with the wrong end date and fixed the next day. With the price overwritten, how do you answer what the shelf showed in between, and what the store believed at the time?
Your valid-from tells you when a price was in force. How do you tell a price that was always in force from one entered late and back-dated?
A store exception, a zone rollback and the online price all apply to one item today. Which rows does your table hold, and which one does a pickup order use?
A rollback starts at the start of Friday in each store's local day. Stores span several time zones. What do you store, and what does a national report at 23:30 UTC show?
How many rows is that per day at {{stores}} stores, and which events force a recompute of the past?

incidents: After a re-zoning of {{price_zones}} zones, a merchant's report of last quarter's rollback prices changed: the store-to-zone mapping had been stored on the store row and overwritten.

A batch of rollback end dates was loaded in UTC instead of store-local time. In the westernmost stores the rollback ended at the register several hours early on its last day, and the shelf labels still showed the rollback price.

A clearance price and a rollback were both active for the same item in 400 stores because two teams entered them on the same day. The page showed the rollback with a "was" price lower than the clearance price.

templates.title: Store fulfilment as data — orders picked in stores, totes, staging, handoffs and substitutions per line
templates.subtopic: order lines to picks, totes and staging, substitution as its own record, handoff outcomes, aggregate-only operations metrics

sections.scenario: Online grocery orders are picked in {{stores}} stores and handed to customers at a pickup bay or to a delivery driver. There are about {{orders_per_day}} orders a day with about {{lines_per_order}} lines each. Store teams pick several orders in one walk, into totes kept apart by temperature zone (ambient, chilled, frozen). When a tote is full or the walk ends, it goes to a staging location: a shelf, a cooler or a freezer. At handoff the order's totes are brought out, the customer is shown any substitutions, and they can accept or reject each one. In this exercise chilled and frozen totes may stay in staging for at most {{staging_limit_minutes}} minutes (this exercise's rule). Customers set a substitution preference per line (allow any, allow only a choice they named, or none) before the order is picked.
sections.problem: Design the data model for store fulfilment, from order lines to what the customer took home. Cover order lines and their requested quantities; pick walks and the picks within them (found, short, or substituted); totes and the lines in them; staging locations and each tote's moves between them; the handoff and the customer's decision on each substitution; weighted items; and the per-line outcome that analytics read. Show the facts and grains that answer, per store and day: fill rate (requested units delivered as ordered), substitution rate and acceptance rate, items short with no substitute offered, and time in staging per temperature zone.
sections.constraints: One line can end up in several states at once: of 6 units, 4 picked as ordered, 1 substituted and 1 short. A substitute is a different item at its own price, linked to the line it replaces; in this exercise the customer pays no more than the price of the item ordered (this exercise's rule). Weighted items (produce, deli) are ordered as an estimate and picked as an actual weight. All operational metrics are reported per store, department and day in aggregate; no individual associate is measured or ranked, and analytics do not carry associate identifiers. Times are reported in the store's local time.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, lines per order, store counts and the staging limit are hypothetical. Payment and refunds are out of scope except for the amount charged per line. Delivery after handoff to the driver is out of scope.
sections.criteria: Requested quantity on the line and outcome rows that reconcile to it; substitution as its own row linking ordered and picked items, with the customer's decision at handoff; totes owned by one order, lines split across totes; staging as timed moves with intervals derived; weighted items with estimated and actual quantities; precise metric definitions and denominators; aggregates per store and day with no associate identifiers in analytics; incremental builds; incidents handled by correction rows and recomputation of the affected days.

clarifications.q: Can one tote hold lines from more than one order?
clarifications.a: During a walk a cart holds several orders' totes, but each tote belongs to exactly one order.

clarifications.q: Can a line be split across totes?
clarifications.a: Yes: a large quantity, or a line moved to a new tote when the first one filled.

clarifications.q: What if the customer rejects a substitute at handoff?
clarifications.a: The substitute goes back to the store, the customer is not charged for it, and for the line the units count as short.

clarifications.q: Can a tote change staging location?
clarifications.a: Yes, for example from a cooler to a pickup bay's cooler when the customer arrives early. Every move has a time.

clarifications.q: Is the picker recorded?
clarifications.a: The operational system needs to know which walk a pick belonged to; analytics never carry who did it.

hints: Keep requested quantity on the line and record every outcome (picked, substituted, short, rejected) as its own row with a quantity, so the line reconciles.
A substitution links two items: the one ordered and the one picked. Model it as a row of its own, not as a changed item id on the line.
Time in staging is a sequence of tote moves; derive intervals from them instead of storing a "staged at" column that is overwritten.
followups: Write the invariant that ties a line's requested units to its outcome rows. What happens to a line whose outcomes do not add up?
A customer ordered 2 kg of apples; 2.3 kg was picked. What is stored, what is charged in this exercise, and how does fill rate treat it?
Define acceptance rate precisely. Is the denominator substitutes offered, substitutes handed out, or lines with a substitute? What happens when the customer never arrives?
A tote of frozen items was moved twice and handed over at {{staging_limit_minutes}} minutes plus 10. Which rows show it, and how do you report breaches per store and day?
At {{orders_per_day}} orders a day, which tables are facts, at what grain, and which one would you keep as an accumulating snapshot per line?

rules.ask: A line of 6 units has 4 picked, 1 substituted and 1 short, and the substitute is then rejected. What does a single status say, and how do you rebuild the line's state at 14:00?
If the substitute's item id replaces the ordered one, how do you report "items short with no substitute offered" and the price cap for the substitute?
Analytics never carry who picked. Which grain do your operational metrics use, and how do you keep identifiers out of the warehouse?
The tote moved from a cooler to a pickup bay cooler. Which interval counts towards the {{staging_limit_minutes}}-minute limit, and how is it computed?
The ordered quantity is an estimate. Which number do fill rate and the charge use, and what if the picked weight is far above the estimate?

incidents: After a handheld app release, rejected substitutes were recorded as accepted for several hours in 300 stores. Acceptance rate for those days is wrong, and customers were charged for items they did not take.
Frozen totes in one region show staging times far above {{staging_limit_minutes}} minutes; a cooler-to-bay move was logged with the store's local time while other moves were in UTC.
At {{orders_per_day}} orders a day, the nightly job that rebuilds the per-line outcome table from all events takes longer every week and missed the morning report twice.

templates.title: Distribution-centre flows as data — receipts, cross-docking, allocations to stores, outbound trailers and units in transit on a date
templates.subtopic: unit conservation across DC stages, cross-dock versus storage, case packs, as-of in-transit queries

sections.scenario: A retailer replenishes {{stores}} stores from {{dcs}} distribution centres that together handle about {{cases_per_day}} cases a day. Inbound loads arrive against purchase orders; each pallet and case carries a scannable label. About {{crossdock_share}} of the cases are cross-docked: already allocated to stores when they arrive, they move straight from receiving to an outbound lane without being stored. The rest are put away into storage and later allocated to stores as replenishment orders come in, picked, and loaded. Outbound trailers carry cases for one or more stores, and each store scans what it receives. Planning, finance and the stores need one consistent answer to "where are the units of item X on date D": received but not allocated, allocated but not shipped, in transit to which store, or received by the store.
sections.problem: Design the data model for flows through the distribution centres. Cover purchase orders and their lines; receipts at pallet and case level; the cross-dock and storage paths; allocations of quantities to stores (made before arrival for cross-dock, after putaway otherwise); picks and loads onto outbound trailers; departures; store receipts with shortages and overages; and case packs and units. Show how "units in transit to each store on date D" and "units at each distribution centre by state on date D" are computed, and how you prove that units are conserved from receipt to store.
sections.constraints: Purchase orders and allocations are in cases, store inventory in units, and an item's case pack can change over time (a supplier moves from 12 to 8 per case); every quantity must be convertible as of the time it was recorded. Every flow is an append-only event with an event time and a recorded time; scans arrive late and sometimes twice. In this exercise conservation holds per distribution centre and item: received = in storage + allocated not shipped + shipped + written off. Store data are reported per store in aggregate. No supplier, carrier or vendor is identified in analytics beyond an id.
sections.assumptions: DC counts, store counts, volumes and the cross-dock share are hypothetical. Returns to suppliers and transfers between distribution centres are out of scope unless you choose to add them.
sections.criteria: Cases as the unit of identity with append-only events and event and recorded times; cross-dock and storage paths in one model; allocations as events in cases with conversion to units by the case pack in force at the time; state on a date from the latest event per case; conservation per distribution centre and item, checked; shortages and overages at store receipt; duplicates handled by event identity; a sound choice between snapshots and on-demand computation; each incident explained and corrected.

clarifications.q: Can a cross-docked case end up in storage?
clarifications.a: Yes, when its trailer is full or the store's allocation is cancelled; it is then put away and re-allocated later.

clarifications.q: Is a store receipt per case or per unit?
clarifications.a: Per case scan; a store can report a case short (not on the trailer) or a damaged case. Overages happen when a case for another store is unloaded by mistake.

clarifications.q: What does "in transit on date D" mean?
clarifications.a: Shipped from a distribution centre at or before the end of D, not yet received by the store at that moment. You choose the time zone and say why.

clarifications.q: Are allocations ever changed?
clarifications.a: Yes, before picking. A changed allocation is a new allocation event, not an edit.

clarifications.q: Does the same label appear twice?
clarifications.a: A case label is unique per case, but scanners resend scans after losing connectivity.

hints: Treat the case label as the unit of identity; every stage is an event on a case (received, put away, allocated, picked, loaded, departed, received at store).
A state on date D is the latest event per case at or before D; counts by state come from that, never from a mutable "current location" column alone.
Convert cases to units with the case pack in force when the case was received, not today's.
followups: Write the query that returns units in transit per store and item at the end of D. Which event table and which "latest event" rule does it use?
A case pack changed from 12 to 8 last month. Cases received before the change are still in storage. How many units does the distribution centre hold, and what does the store's receipt show?
A trailer arrives at a store with two cases missing and one case for another store. Which rows are written, and how does conservation still hold for each store and distribution centre?
At {{cases_per_day}} cases a day, would you keep a daily snapshot of each case's state, or compute states from events on demand? What does each cost?
Scans arrive up to two days late. When is "in transit on D" final, and what do you show planners before then?

rules.ask: Planning asks how many units were in transit to a store last Tuesday at midnight. With a single current location column, how do you answer?
The store's inventory is in units and a case pack changed last month. Which case pack converts a case received before the change, and where is that stored?
A scanner resends a "loaded" scan two hours later. What key makes it a duplicate rather than a second load, and what if the case really was loaded twice after being unloaded?
A cross-docked case misses its trailer and is put away. How do its allocation and its state change, and how is that visible in the cross-dock share you report?
How many case-state rows is that per day at {{cases_per_day}} cases, and how do late scans correct a snapshot already taken?

incidents: Units in transit to stores jumped 30% overnight at one distribution centre: its scanners resent a day of "loaded" scans after a network outage, and the count summed loads instead of taking the latest state per case.

After a case pack change, a store's receipts in units disagreed with the distribution centre's shipments by a third for that item; the conversion used the current case pack for cases shipped before the change.

With {{crossdock_share}} of cases cross-docked, a week of cancelled store allocations left thousands of cases with no allocation and no storage location; they appear in no state, and conservation fails for those items.

templates.title: Marketplace offers as data — many sellers per item, the featured offer chosen by a given rule, and its history
templates.subtopic: offer versions, eligibility inputs, featured-offer intervals, explainable selections, what the customer saw at order time

featured_rule: the lowest total price (item price plus shipping) among eligible offers, ties going to the earliest delivery promise
the highest value of a score you are given per offer, recomputed whenever price, stock or delivery promise changes

sections.scenario: An online catalogue holds about {{items}} items, and many are sold by several marketplace sellers as well as by the retailer itself. There are about {{sellers}} active sellers, and offers change about {{offer_updates}} times a day: price, shipping price, quantity available, delivery promise, condition. Only one offer per item is featured on the item page, and in this exercise it is chosen by {{featured_rule}} (this exercise's rule; check current docs). An offer is eligible only if it is in stock, new (not refurbished) and its seller meets published performance minimums such as on-time delivery and valid tracking rates (this exercise's eligibility rule). Sellers ask why they lost the featured offer; category managers ask how often the retailer's own offer is featured; customer care asks what a customer saw when they ordered.
sections.problem: Design the data model for marketplace offers and the featured offer. Cover the item and its variants; sellers and their performance standing over time; offers and every version of an offer; eligibility as computed at a moment, with the reasons; the featured-offer decision as intervals per item, with the inputs that produced it; and the link from an order line to the offer and featured state at order time. Show the queries for: the share of time and of orders each seller's offer was featured per item and week, and "why was seller S not featured on item X at time T".
sections.constraints: Offer versions are append-only with event time and recorded time; a seller can send updates out of order. A selection must be reproducible: from the stored inputs you can recompute exactly the offer the rule chose. A seller sees only their own offers' data and aggregate competition facts the rule exposes (for example, the featured price), never another seller's details. Money is stored in integer cents.
sections.assumptions: Catalogue size, seller counts, update volume and the rule are hypothetical. Search ranking and advertising are out of scope. The retailer's own offer is modelled as an offer from one more seller.
sections.criteria: Items, sellers, seller standing over time, and append-only offer versions with event and recorded times; eligibility computed with reasons; featured-offer decisions as non-overlapping intervals per item referring to the offer versions and inputs that produced them, including "none eligible"; reproducible selections under the stated rule; order lines linked to the offer version and featured state at order time; seller-scoped views; share-of-time queries that split intervals at week boundaries; incidents explained and repaired by recomputing intervals from stored inputs.

clarifications.q: Is the featured offer stored or computed on read?
clarifications.a: Your choice; the history must exist either way.

clarifications.q: Does a seller's performance standing change often?
clarifications.a: In this exercise it is recomputed daily over a trailing window, so eligibility can change at a day boundary with no change to the offer itself.

clarifications.q: What if no offer is eligible?
clarifications.a: The item page shows no featured offer in this exercise; that is a state to record, not a gap.

clarifications.q: Can two offers tie?
clarifications.a: Yes. The rule's tie-break decides, and if it still ties, the earlier offer wins; say how you would record that.

clarifications.q: Does an order record the offer it bought?
clarifications.a: It records the offer id; whether it also records the offer version is your decision.

hints: Store offer versions, not offers with mutable columns; the featured decision then refers to the versions it compared.
Featured history is a set of intervals per item: (item, offer, valid_from, valid_to, reason). Intervals make "share of time" a sum of durations.
Eligibility has its own inputs (stock, condition, seller standing); record the failing reason per offer at each decision.
followups: Write the query for each seller's share of featured time per item and week, including intervals that cross a week boundary.
A seller's update arrives 10 minutes late: its price dropped at 12:00 but the system learned at 12:10. Who was featured between 12:00 and 12:10 in your history, and in what the customer saw?
Seller standing is recomputed at midnight and three sellers become ineligible. How many decisions are recomputed, and how do you avoid re-evaluating every item?
A seller disputes that they lost the featured offer unfairly last Tuesday at 15:00. Produce the evidence from your tables, showing only what that seller is allowed to see.
At {{offer_updates}} updates a day, how do you store offer versions and featured intervals so that both the history queries and the item page stay fast?

rules.ask: A seller asks why they lost the featured offer at 15:00 last Tuesday. With offers overwritten, what can you show them?
A flag on the offer row says who is featured now. How do you compute each seller's share of featured time last week, and how do you avoid two offers flagged at once?
Which time does the featured history use, and which does "what the customer saw" use? Can they disagree, and which is right for which question?
The score you are given is recomputed by another team. Which score value and version does your decision row keep, so the selection can be reproduced later?
A seller's view of a lost decision must not reveal a competitor's details. Which columns do they see, and how is that enforced?

incidents: With {{offer_updates}} updates a day, a backlog delayed price updates by 40 minutes during a holiday sale. Featured history built from recorded time shows sellers losing the featured offer for prices they had already lowered.
A daily standing recomputation marked 2,000 sellers ineligible because a tracking-rate input was missing for one day. Their offers lost the featured position on thousands of items until the next run.
Featured-time shares for one category add up to 107% per item and week: intervals were closed with the next decision's recorded time, while new ones started at event time, so they overlap.

templates.title: Rollback lift — units per store-day against the four weeks before, out-of-stock days left out
templates.subtopic: store-day calendars, missing zero rows, exclusions on both sides, date windows, NULL-safe ratios

sections.scenario: A retailer runs rollbacks: a temporary lower price on one item in every store of one region, from start_date to end_date (this exercise's rule; check current docs for how a real programme works). {{region_rule}} Merchandising wants a first readout of each rollback: did the item sell more per store and day during the rollback than in the four weeks before it? A store-day when the item was out of stock says nothing about demand, so in this exercise it is left out on both sides. The sample covers {{first_day}} to {{last_day}}.
sections.problem:
Write one PostgreSQL query that returns, for every rollback, rollback_id, item_id, rollback_store_days, rollback_units_per_store_day, baseline_store_days, baseline_units_per_store_day, lift_pct, ordered by rollback_id.

  • A rollback's store-days are the pairs (store, date) where the store is in the rollback's region and the date is in a window. The rollback window is start_date through end_date; the baseline window is the 28 days before it, start_date − 28 through start_date − 1. Both are inclusive dates.
  • A store-day counts only on or after the store's opened_on. It is left out when the item has a row in out_of_stock_days for that store and date, and so are its units, even if some sold before the shelf emptied. {{overlap_rule}}
  • {{rows_rule}}
  • *_store_days is the number of counted store-days. *_units_per_store_day is the units sold on the counted store-days divided by that number, rounded to 2 decimals; the baseline's is NULL when it has no counted store-days.
  • lift_pct is 100 × (rollback rate ÷ baseline rate − 1), computed from the unrounded rates and rounded to 1 decimal; NULL when the baseline rate is 0 or NULL.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Dates are calendar dates in each store's local time and are stored as DATE; no time zone conversion is needed. Use ROUND(numeric, n). The sample has {{rollback_count}} rollbacks and {{sales_rows}} sales rows; production has thousands of stores and hundreds of thousands of items, with a rollback readout due every morning.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, regions, stores, items, prices and units. A rollback's price is shown for context and plays no part in the calculation. This readout is a simple before-and-after comparison, not a causal estimate; holdout stores and seasonality are discussed in the follow-ups.
sections.criteria: Store-days built from a calendar and the stores in the rollback's region, not from sales rows; opening dates, out-of-stock days and (hardest level) other rollbacks of the item removed with their units; inclusive windows with the baseline ending the day before the start; numeric division with NULL-safe lift from unrounded rates; deterministic order; can discuss holdout comparisons, cannibalisation, finer out-of-stock signals and incremental materialisation.

clarifications.q: Is end_date part of the rollback?
clarifications.a: Yes. Both windows are inclusive at both ends.

clarifications.q: What if an item sold some units and then ran out the same day?
clarifications.a: The day has a row in out_of_stock_days, so the whole store-day is left out, units included.

clarifications.q: Should stores outside the rollback's region count in its baseline?
clarifications.a: No. Both windows use only the stores in the rollback's region.

clarifications.q: The baseline sold nothing at all. What is the lift?
