clarifications.a: NULL. The baseline rate is 0.00 and a ratio to zero means nothing.

clarifications.q: Do I round the rates before computing lift?
clarifications.a: No. Compute lift from the unrounded rates and round each output once.

hints: Build the store-days first: each rollback's two windows, joined to the stores in its region, expanded to one row per date (generate_series over the day offsets, or a calendar table).
Remove the store-days that do not count (before opening, out of stock, and any other exclusion the statement names) with NOT EXISTS, then LEFT JOIN the sales and sum with COALESCE(units, 0).
Aggregate per rollback and window, then put the two windows side by side. units::numeric / store_days avoids integer division.
followups: Some rollbacks run in regions where the item sold strongly before for seasonal reasons. How would you compare against holdout stores instead of the item's own past, and what must be decided before the rollback starts?
A rollback lifted the item by 60%, but sales of a similar item in the same stores fell. How would you extend the query to show that?
Out-of-stock days are flagged per whole day here. With an hourly on-shelf signal, how would the denominator change, and is it worth it?
This query recomputes every rollback from raw daily sales each morning. At production scale, what would you materialise, at what grain, and what forces a recompute?

rules.ask: Which rows does your AVG run over? A store-day with no sales row is not in the sales table at all; does it count as a zero in your average?
Which store-days disappear when you start from the sales table, and which way does that bias both rates?
Show your baseline window's last day. Is the rollback's first day inside it?
How many rows does your calendar produce for one rollback in production, with a thousand stores in a region, and how would you avoid building it per rollback?
What happens to NOT IN if the subquery ever returns a NULL, and would NOT EXISTS be safer here?

incidents: A merchant shows a rollback with lift above 400% in one region. A data feed had stopped writing zero-sale days for weeks, and a version of this report that averaged only the rows present overstated both rates differently.
Out-of-stock flags for one region arrived a day late, so the morning readout counted empty-shelf days at the rollback price as demand and showed a lower lift than the corrected readout an hour later.

templates.title: Near-real-time store inventory across thousands of stores, corrected by cycle counts
templates.subtopic: perpetual inventory, count corrections, late data, availability shown online

sections.scenario: A retailer runs {{stores}} stores, each carrying about {{items_per_store}} items, and sells online for delivery and for pickup at a store. Online shoppers who choose a store see each item as "in stock", "limited stock" or "out of stock" there. A store's on-hand quantity for an item changes all day: register sales and returns, receipts from distribution centres, transfers between stores, damaged and expired units written off, units picked for online orders, and cycle counts in which store teams count a shelf or a backroom location and the count corrects the system's number. Together these come to about {{events}} inventory-affecting events a day. The perpetual on-hand should reflect a register sale within {{freshness}}.
sections.problem: Design the store inventory system: ingestion from registers, handheld devices and receiving; the perpetual on-hand per store and item, and where it lives; how a cycle count corrects it while the store is open and selling; the availability state shown online and the rule behind it; the read path for product and search pages; and how inventory accuracy is measured per store and category. Say what is exact, what is approximate, and how fresh each number is.
sections.constraints: Registers and handheld devices buffer events while offline and upload them later, sometimes hours later; events can arrive out of order and twice. A count is a snapshot at one moment, and sales keep happening during and after it. Online availability reads must answer p99 under 50 ms at holiday peak. Showing "in stock" for an item that is not on the shelf leads to a failed pick and a disappointed pickup customer; hiding an item that is there loses a sale. Accuracy is reported per store, department and category in aggregate; no individual associate's counts are measured or ranked.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, timings and thresholds are hypothetical, and the three online states and their thresholds are this exercise's rule. Every event carries an event id, store, item, quantity change, reason, the device time and the time it was received. A count carries the store, item, location (sales floor, backroom, a second display), the counted quantity and the count time. Receipts arrive in cases and are converted to units using the item's pack size.
sections.criteria: On-hand as a projection of an append-only, idempotent event log keyed by store and item; counts applied as a balance at the count time with later changes replayed on top, so late events neither double count nor vanish; event-time ordering per store and item with duplicate handling by event id; online state derived from on-hand, units held for unpicked orders and a buffer that adapts to measured reliability; a fast, regionally served read view refreshed within the freshness target, with exact checks at picking; accuracy defined precisely and reported in aggregate only; pack-size conversion versioned by effective date; sanity checks on counts (large swings, device time); rebuild by replay beside the live view; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is a count always right?
clarifications.a: It is the best evidence at its moment, but people miscount and scan the wrong item. Decide how far you trust one count.

clarifications.q: Does a count cover every location of the item in the store?
clarifications.a: Not always; some counts cover one location. Say how you combine them.

clarifications.q: Do online orders hold stock before they are picked?
clarifications.a: Orders awaiting picking are known by store and item; picking itself decrements on-hand. You may hold back units for orders not yet picked.

clarifications.q: Does the online page show quantities?
clarifications.a: No, only the three states. You propose the rule that maps a number to a state.

clarifications.q: Can an item's pack size change?
clarifications.a: Yes, occasionally, and the change can arrive after cases with the new size have been received.

hints: Keep on-hand as a projection of an append-only event log per store and item, so any balance can be rebuilt and every unit change traced to its event.
A count taken at time T sets the balance as of T, not as of now: on-hand = counted quantity + the sum of changes with event time after T. Changes timed before T that arrive late must not move it.
The state shown online can depend on more than on-hand: units held for unpicked orders, and how reliable that store's number for that item has been.
followups: A count of 12 is recorded at 10:05. Sales scanned at 10:02, 10:07 and 10:09 arrive at 10:20. What is on-hand afterwards, and why?
How do you define and measure inventory accuracy per store and category, and what would make that metric misleading?
How do you choose the buffer that keeps an item from showing "in stock" when it is probably not on the shelf, and how would you know it is too cautious?
A store's network is down for two hours. What does the online page show for that store meanwhile, and what happens when its events arrive?
A bug applied one reason code with the wrong sign for a day in every store. How do you rebuild every affected balance without stopping the read path?

rules.ask: A count overwrites on-hand at 10:05. Sales scanned at 10:02 arrive at 10:20. Does your design subtract them a second time?
What do you key the stream by? One store uploads three hours of backlog at once; what happens to the freshness of every other store on that partition?
A popular item sells its last unit at 14:00. How long does your cached state keep saying "in stock", and how many pickup orders can be placed in that time?
A fixed buffer of two units hides every item a small store stocks only one or two of. How would your buffer adapt to the item and the store?
A sale must show within {{freshness}}. Which parts of your design can still run nightly, and which cannot?

incidents: One store's registers are offline for three hours on a busy Saturday, then upload 40,000 sales at once. Meanwhile online shoppers saw "in stock" for items that had sold out, and pickup orders for them failed at picking.

A handheld app release records count times in UTC but labels them as store local time. In stores west of UTC each count is treated as taken hours later than it was, sales made in between are ignored, and on-hand reads high for every counted item.

Inventory accuracy for one category drops across most of the {{stores}} stores overnight. The item's pack size changed from 12 to 6 units a case, and cases received since are being converted at the old size.
A count with a mis-scanned barcode sets one item to 0 and a similar item to 48 in the same store; the first disappears from the online page for that store.

templates.title: Returns across channels — refunds, restock or disposal, and sales and inventory restated
templates.subtopic: returns linked to original sales, dispositions, restatement and closed periods

sections.scenario: A retailer with {{stores}} stores accepts about {{returns_per_day}} returns a day. An item bought in a store can be returned in any store; an online order, whether shipped from a distribution centre or picked in a store for pickup or delivery, can be returned in a store or by mail to a returns centre; some marketplace sellers' items can be returned in a store too. In this exercise an item may be returned within {{window_days}} days of purchase (this exercise's rule; check current docs). Each return produces a refund to the original payment method, and the returned unit gets a disposition: back on the shelf, back to the supplier, sold through a liquidation channel, donated, or destroyed. Finance closes each month {{close_days}} business days after it ends, and closed numbers do not change.
sections.problem: Design the returns data system: capture at store service desks, registers and returns centres; linking each returned unit to its original order line and the price actually paid; the refund events; dispositions and the inventory changes they cause; and how sales are restated, including which store, channel and day carry a return. State the reporting rule precisely and explain how it treats returns that arrive after a month has closed.
sections.constraints: A return can be partial (two of five units), part of a bundle, or for an item bought with a discount that applied to the whole order. Refunds are integer cents and must equal what the customer actually paid for the returned units. A store that takes back an online order receives inventory it never received from a distribution centre. Customer data appear only in aggregate in analytics; refund amounts are reconciled with the payments system daily. Store results are reported per store and day in each store's local time.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, windows and timings are hypothetical, and the return window, disposition codes and restatement rule are this exercise's. Every return event carries a return id, the original order or receipt reference when there is one, the item, the quantity, where it was returned, the refund amount and tender, and a disposition that may be recorded hours or days later.
sections.criteria: Separate, linked records for refund, unit and restatement with their own timestamps and owners; returns linked to the original order line with discounts allocated to lines at sale time and exact integer-cent refunds; a precise, stated restatement rule (for example, the return reduces the original channel in finance views and is shown separately as "returns accepted" in the receiving store's view) applied by the receiving store's local day; idempotent capture by return id; inventory moves only on dispositions, with "pending disposition" as a visible state; closed periods immutable, late returns booked in the open period with a reference; daily reconciliation with the payments system; customer data in aggregate only; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Which store and channel does a return reduce: where it was bought, or where it was returned?
clarifications.a: Finance and store operations disagree. Propose a rule and say what each audience sees.

clarifications.q: Is a return always linked to an original sale?
clarifications.a: Usually; returns without a receipt happen and get a looked-up or a current price under this exercise's rule.

clarifications.q: Who funds a marketplace item's refund?
clarifications.a: The seller, under the marketplace's terms; the retailer may refund first and recover it. Keep the two flows separate.

clarifications.q: When is a disposition known?
clarifications.a: Restock is often recorded at the desk; others are decided later at a returns centre, sometimes days later.

clarifications.q: Can a refund be issued without the item being returned?
clarifications.a: Yes, for some low-value items or damaged deliveries, under this exercise's rule. No inventory moves.

hints: Separate the facts: the refund (money), the unit (inventory and disposition) and the sales restatement (reporting). They happen at different times and are owned by different systems.
Allocate order-level discounts to lines when the sale happens, so a return can be valued from the line without recomputing the order.
A closed period never changes; a late return lands in the open period with a reference to the period it relates to.
followups: An online order of five units with a 10% order discount is partly returned in a store: two units. What refund is issued, and which rows change in sales, inventory and refunds?
Which store's sales does an online return made in a store reduce, and what does the store manager's daily report show?
A disposition arrives four days after the refund. How do on-hand and the returns-centre backlog look in between?
How do you reconcile refunds in your data with what the payments system actually paid out, and what do you do with the difference?

Finance asks for return rates by category and channel that do not move after a month is closed. How do you provide them, and what do you say about returns still to come within the {{window_days}}-day window?

rules.ask: An online order is returned in a store. The store's own sales for the day fall. How do you keep the store's report fair while finance still sees net sales by channel?
You update the original sale row when it is returned. What does last month's report show if someone re-runs it after the close?
A unit is marked "restock" at the desk but sits in the backroom for three days. What does the online page show for that store meanwhile?
About 3% of returns have no receipt reference. How do you value them, and how do they appear in return rates?
An order discount of 100 cents is spread over three lines. How do you allocate it so the line refunds add back to exactly what was paid?

incidents: Online orders returned in stores are counted as negative in-store sales. Store comparable sales fall about 2% in a month with heavy online returns, while online net sales look overstated by the same amount.
After a network blip, one store's service desk sends each of 900 return events twice. The payments system refunded each once, but the units are restocked twice and on-hand for those items reads high.

A returns centre clears a backlog of 60,000 mail-in returns on the first day of a new month, after the previous month has closed. The new month's online net sales start negative in two categories, and a merchant asks why.

A register release records refunds for no-receipt returns at the item's current price instead of the price under this exercise's rule; refunds no longer reconcile with the payments system by a few thousand dollars a day.

templates.title: Pickup and delivery slot capacity — honest availability at peak
templates.subtopic: multi-dimensional capacity, contention at peak, holds, honest availability

sections.scenario: Online grocery customers at {{stores}} stores choose a pickup or delivery slot at checkout: a {{slot_minutes}}-minute window, offered up to {{days_ahead}} days ahead. Each slot's capacity is limited in several ways at once: the picking hours the store has planned for that period (planned in aggregate, not per person), chilled and frozen staging space for totes, pickup parking bays, and delivery routes. In the week before a holiday, booking attempts peak at {{peak_bookings}} a minute, and the most popular slots fill within seconds of opening. A slot chosen at checkout is held for {{hold_minutes}} minutes while the customer finishes paying (this exercise's rule). Customers can change their order until a cut-off before the slot. Showing a slot as available that then fails at checkout frustrates customers; showing a slot as full when it is not loses orders.
sections.problem: Design the slot capacity system: the capacity model and its units; how a store's capacity is set and changed during the day; the booking path (hold, confirm, release, change, cancel) and what makes it exact; the availability read path at peak; and the metrics that tell you whether availability is honest. Say what happens to already booked orders when a store's capacity drops.
sections.constraints: A slot may never be booked beyond its capacity plus the overbooking allowance the store sets (zero by default). The availability read path must handle several times the booking rate, p99 under 100 ms. Slots are in each store's local time, including on the days clocks change. Order size varies widely, and a large order uses more picking time and more totes than a small one. Store data are reported per store and slot in aggregate.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, windows and rules are hypothetical. Each store publishes its planned capacity per slot and resource; it can change it during the day, for example after bad weather or when fewer people are available than planned. Each order carries an estimated picking time and tote count by temperature zone, refined as the order changes.
sections.criteria: A capacity model in the limiting resources (picking minutes, totes per temperature zone, bays, route stops) with order estimates refined on change; an exact booking path using conditional decrements and idempotent hold, confirm and release by order id, with holds that expire by rule and count as free when past their deadline; hot-slot contention handled (sharded counters or a single writer per store-slot, plus a waiting room or fair queue at opening); an availability view with stated staleness, a near-full margin, and a re-check at booking; honest-availability metrics (failed-on-shown-available rate, fill time, idle capacity); capacity reductions handled by a visible, prioritised re-slotting with customer notice; local-time slot generation correct across daylight-saving changes; aggregate reporting only; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is capacity a number of orders?
clarifications.a: That is your choice. A count of orders is simple; picking minutes and totes are closer to the real limits. Say what you lose either way.

clarifications.q: Does a hold use capacity?
clarifications.a: Yes, for {{hold_minutes}} minutes; then it is released if checkout has not completed.

clarifications.q: What if a customer adds many items after booking?
clarifications.a: Changes are allowed until the cut-off; say whether the slot can refuse them or what else happens.

clarifications.q: Can a delivery slot be served from another store?
clarifications.a: In some areas two stores overlap; you may propose using that.

clarifications.q: What happens when capacity drops below what is already booked?
clarifications.a: Someone must decide which orders move; the system must make that decision visible and fast.

hints: Separate the exact booking path, which decrements capacity with a conditional write, from the availability view, which can be slightly stale but must say how stale.
Measure capacity in the resource that runs out first: picking minutes, totes per temperature zone, bays or route stops. An order consumes some of each.
Honest availability is measurable: of the slots shown as available, what share failed when the customer tried to book them?
followups: Walk through one booking for a popular slot: which records change, in what order, and what makes two racing customers unable to take the last capacity?
The availability view is a few seconds stale at peak. How do you keep shown-available slots from failing at checkout too often?
A store reduces capacity for tomorrow's busiest slot by a third. Which booked orders move, who decides, and what do customers see?
A customer adds forty items an hour before the cut-off. What happens to the slot's capacity and to other customers?
How do you decide each store's capacity per slot next week, and how do you learn from slots that were overfull or idle?

rules.ask: Thousands of customers try the 18:00 Saturday slot in the same second. How long do they wait on that lock, and what do the others see?
The cache says the slot has capacity, the booking path says it is full. What does the customer see, and how often does that happen at peak?
Who gets the next free capacity, the customer who joined first or the one whose retry happened to arrive? Does that matter here?
On the night clocks go back, the 01:00 hour happens twice. Which slots exist that night, and what does a customer see?
A holiday order is three times the usual size. What does your order count do to picking and staging in that slot?

incidents: In the week before a holiday the availability view is refreshed every 60 seconds. Thirty percent of booking attempts fail on slots shown as available; customers retry, and booking traffic triples.
A storm closes a store's parking lot for an afternoon. The store cuts the 16:00 to 18:00 pickup capacity by half, and 140 orders are already booked into it.
On the day clocks change, slots are generated in UTC and converted once at midnight; one store shows a slot that starts at a time that does not exist and no slot for an hour that does.
Holiday orders average twice the usual tote count. Every {{slot_minutes}}-minute slot books to its order limit, and chilled staging overflows by mid-afternoon in most stores.

templates.title: In-transit visibility for store replenishment — trailers, ETAs and receiving plans
templates.subtopic: trip tracking, ETA updates with hysteresis, manifests, units in transit

sections.scenario: A retailer replenishes {{stores}} stores from {{dcs}} distribution centres, with about {{trips}} trailer trips a day. A trip can serve one store or several in sequence, and its manifest lists the pallets and cases for each stop. Trailers report their position every {{ping_minutes}} minutes through a common tracking feed, plus events for departure, arrival at a stop, door open and door close; refrigerated trailers also report temperature. Stores plan their receiving around expected arrivals: an unloading window, the stocking hours they plan in aggregate, chilled and frozen items first, and backroom space. Replenishment ordering counts units already in transit so a store is not sent the same need twice.
sections.problem: Design the in-transit visibility system: ingestion of positions and trip events; the state of each trip and each stop; the ETA per stop and how it is updated; the units in transit per store and item from manifests; how store receiving plans are told about changes; how receipts at the store close out the manifest, including shortages and overages; and how ETA accuracy is measured per distribution centre and route type. Say which numbers other systems may depend on and how fresh each one is.
sections.constraints: Trailers lose signal in some areas; position reports arrive late, out of order and sometimes twice. A store's receiving plan should change only when an ETA change matters to it, not on every position report. Manifests are in cases; store inventory is in units. A trailer's temperature outside its allowed range for too long means its perishable items must be inspected at receipt (this exercise's rule). Store results are reported per store and day in aggregate.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, intervals and thresholds are hypothetical. Trailers are run by the retailer's own fleet and by outside carriers, and in this exercise all report through one feed in one format; nothing here describes any company's fleet, carriers or tracking provider. Every report carries a trailer id, a trip id when known, a position or event, a device time and the time it was received.
sections.criteria: An event-time trip and stop state machine that late or duplicate reports cannot regress; ETAs computed from positions and remaining stops, published with hysteresis and a materiality threshold tied to the store's planning lead time; feed health monitored per source with a "position unknown since" state and conservative ETAs when stale; units in transit from manifests (converted to units) cleared by store receipt scans, with manifest reconciliation recording shortages and overages and correcting both stores; replenishment counting in-transit units with a rule for late and lost shipments; temperature excursions evaluated by event time and routed to receipt inspection even when late; an ETA accuracy metric at a fixed horizon; aggregate store reporting; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Who computes the ETA?
clarifications.a: You do, from positions, the remaining stops and typical travel and unloading times. Say what inputs you use.

clarifications.q: How early does a store need to know about a delay?
clarifications.a: About two hours before the planned window, to move its unloading hours; changes of under 30 minutes do not matter to it.

clarifications.q: Can a pallet be unloaded at the wrong stop?
clarifications.a: It happens. The receiving store scans what it gets, and the next store finds it missing.

clarifications.q: When does a unit stop being "in transit"?
clarifications.a: That is your rule to define; the replenishment calculation depends on it.

clarifications.q: What if a trailer's feed stops?
clarifications.a: Positions stop; the trailer keeps moving. Decide what you show and when you start to worry.

hints: Model the trip as a state machine per stop (planned, departed, approaching, arrived, unloading, closed), driven by event time, so late reports never move it backwards.
Separate the raw ETA, which can move with every report, from the ETA you publish to stores, which changes only past a threshold and with a reason.
Units leave "in transit" when the store scans them in, not when the trailer arrives; reconcile the manifest against the scans and record the differences.
followups: A position report from 40 minutes ago arrives after the trailer's arrival event. What changes, and what does not?
How do you publish ETAs to stores so their plans do not change with every report, while a real two-hour delay still reaches them in time?
Pallets for the second stop are unloaded at the first. What do units in transit, the two stores' on-hand and the replenishment calculation show, and how is it corrected?
How do you measure ETA accuracy so that it is useful to stores, for example at a fixed time before arrival?
The tracking feed for a group of trailers stops for three hours. What do you show, and how does the system recover when the backlog arrives?

rules.ask: A report from 40 minutes ago arrives after newer ones. Does your trip state or ETA go backwards?
How many ETA notifications does a store get on a normal day under your rule, and which ones does it act on?
What do you key by: trailer, trip or store? A multi-stop trip affects several stores; how does each store's plan see it?
A trailer waits in the store's lot for an hour before its door opens. Has it arrived, and what does your ETA accuracy metric say?
Units are on a trailer that is three hours late. Does replenishment order them again for that store? Why or why not?

incidents: The tracking feed for one region's trailers stops updating for three hours. Their ETAs stay at "on time"; stores keep unloading hours ready for trailers that are delayed, and other stores are not warned of late arrivals.

On a multi-stop trip, pallets for the second store are unloaded at the first. The first store shows an overage, the second a shortage, and the second store's units in transit vanish while nothing arrives.
On routes with heavy traffic, the published ETA swings between "on time" and "40 minutes late" with almost every report, and some stores' receiving plans are changed six times in an afternoon.
A refrigerated trailer reports temperatures above its range for 50 minutes; the reports arrive after the trailer has been unloaded and its chilled items are already on the shelf.

templates.title: Price and promotion analytics — rollbacks, clearance, price matches and lift against holdout stores
templates.subtopic: effective price history, holdout stores, lift with confounders

sections.scenario: A retailer sets prices for {{stores}} stores and its website, nationally and by price zone, with about {{price_changes}} store-item price changes a week. In this exercise there are three kinds of reduction: a rollback, a temporary lower price that runs for {{weeks}} weeks; clearance, a permanent markdown to sell through an item being discontinued; and a price match, in which a store matches a qualifying competitor's advertised price at the register when a customer asks (all three are this exercise's rules; check current docs). Merchants want to know what each rollback achieved: incremental units, sales and margin. To measure it fairly, {{holdout_share}} of stores are held out of selected rollbacks by design and keep the regular price.
sections.problem: Design the price and promotion analytics system: the effective price history per store, item and channel, both as planned and as actually charged at the register; promotions as data; how holdout stores are chosen and recorded; how lift is computed per rollback, with its uncertainty; how out-of-stock days, overlapping promotions, cannibalisation of similar items and seasonality are handled; and how results reach merchants, and how fresh they are.
sections.constraints: Price changes take effect at a store-local time and are sometimes applied late or not at all at a store; the register's charged price is the evidence. Holdout assignment must be decided before the rollback starts and recorded. Lift is reported only per item and region with enough stores to be meaningful; store data appear only in aggregate. Results for a rollback are expected within two days of its end, and must be reproducible later.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, shares and durations are hypothetical; the rollback, clearance, price-match and holdout rules are this exercise's. Register line items carry the store, item, quantity, the shelf price, the price charged and a reason code for any override. Daily store-item on-hand snapshots are available.
sections.criteria: Planned and charged price histories per store, item and channel, versioned with store-local effective times; promotions, clearance and price matches kept distinct by reason; holdout stores chosen by a stated, stratified or matched method before launch, recorded, and verified from register prices; lift as a difference in differences with out-of-stock store-days excluded in both groups, seasonality handled through the comparison, cannibalisation and overlap reported rather than hidden, and uncertainty shown; minimum group sizes and aggregate-only reporting; reproducible results from snapshotted inputs; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Who chooses the holdout stores?
clarifications.a: You propose the method; merchants must agree before launch, and stores must not be told which they are.

clarifications.q: Is the online price part of the test?
clarifications.a: Online prices may follow the rollback nationally. Say how that affects a store-level comparison.

clarifications.q: Are price matches promotions?
clarifications.a: No; they are register overrides. They must not be counted as rollbacks, but they change the price charged.

clarifications.q: What period is the baseline?
clarifications.a: Your choice; say how you handle seasonality and the weeks just before a holiday.

clarifications.q: Do merchants want margin?
clarifications.a: Yes: lift in units and sales, and the margin given up on units that would have sold anyway.

hints: Keep two price histories per store, item and channel: planned (from price files) and charged (from the registers). Most surprises live in the gap between them.
Compare test and holdout stores before and after the rollback starts (a difference in differences), using stores matched or stratified by size, region and past sales.
A store-day when the item was out of stock says nothing about demand; exclude it or model it, in both groups.
followups: Define lift for one rollback precisely: which stores, which days, which baseline, and which items count.
How do you choose holdout stores so the comparison is fair, and how do you check after launch that they really kept the regular price?
The rollback item gains 40% but a similar item from another brand loses 25%. What do you report to the merchant?
Two promotions overlap on the same item in some stores. How do you attribute the lift, or decide not to?
A merchant wants every rollback's lift live, daily, for every store. What do you offer instead, and why?

rules.ask: Random assignment over {{holdout_share}} of stores puts three of the region's largest stores in holdout. Is the comparison still fair, and what would you change?
Sales rise during the rollback in every store, holdout ones included, because it is the week before a holiday. What does your before-and-after number claim?
The price file says the rollback started on Monday; registers in 6% of stores charged the old price until Wednesday. Which price does your history use?
How many holdout stores does a rollback need for the interval to be useful, and what do you report when it has fewer?
How do you estimate the margin given up on units that would have sold at the regular price anyway?

incidents: A price file applies one rollback by price zone instead of by store list, so 15% of the holdout stores receive the rollback too. Its measured lift is about half of what similar rollbacks showed.

Price changes that take effect at store-local midnight are stored at midnight UTC. In western stores, the last evening before each rollback is attributed to the rollback price, and the rollback's own last evening to the regular price.
A register release records price-match overrides with the rollback reason code. Rollback counts and lift in one region jump, though no new rollbacks started there.
A {{weeks}}-week rollback item runs out of stock in most test stores by its second week. The lift report shows the rollback lost sales in its second half.

templates.title: Rolling out a workflow change that thousands of stores must adopt
templates.subtopic: pilots, waves, adoption measured in aggregate, feedback and rollback

change: a new way of recording substitutions while picking online grocery orders
a new handheld flow for cycle counts
receiving trailers by scanning pallets instead of every case
pilot_result: the pilot stores improved the target measure, but the time the task takes rose by a fifth
the pilot went well in large stores and badly in small ones
the pilot's numbers looked good, but a third of the pilot stores had quietly gone back to the old process

sections.scenario: Your team built the software and data behind {{change}}. A pilot ran in 25 stores for a month, and {{pilot_result}}. Leadership wants the change in all {{stores}} stores within {{weeks}} weeks. Store teams are busy, the change alters work they do every day, and the people doing it were not in the room when it was designed. You lead the technical side of the rollout and are accountable for whether it works.
sections.problem: How do you lead the rollout? Cover what you do about the pilot result before going wider, how you decide the waves and what stops the next one, how you measure adoption and outcome without measuring or ranking individual people, how store teams' feedback reaches your team and changes the product, what support and training exist, and how you would pause or roll back. Then tell me about a real time you rolled out a change that many people had to adopt, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Adoption and outcome are measured per store, region and store format in aggregate; no individual associate is measured, ranked or singled out. Stores cannot be offline for training, and a peak season starts soon after the target date. You do not manage store operations; their leaders decide store priorities.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Investigates the pilot result before scaling (time per task, store-format differences, quiet reversion treated as product feedback), with visits or calls to pilot stores alongside store operations; waves chosen across store formats with explicit entry and exit criteria agreed in advance and a named person who can stop them; adoption and outcome measured in aggregate per store and region, explicitly refusing per-associate tracking; feedback loops that change the product (in-app feedback, regional calls, a fast fix cadence); support and lightweight training that fit store work; a tested pause and rollback path and a decision on the old process; a realistic view of the deadline against peak season, raised with evidence; real example with personal contribution and what changed, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is the deadline fixed?
clarifications.a: Leadership chose it; it can move with evidence, through your manager and store operations leadership.

clarifications.q: Can the old process stay available?
clarifications.a: Technically yes, for a while; running both costs support time and muddies the numbers.

clarifications.q: Who talks to stores?
clarifications.a: Store operations and regional leaders. Your team can join calls and visit stores with them.

clarifications.q: What does the pilot data cover?
clarifications.a: Per-store aggregates of the target measure, time per task, and errors, plus written feedback from pilot stores.

hints: Understand the pilot result before scaling it: what explains it, and does it hold in every store format?
Decide in advance what each wave must show before the next starts, and who can stop it.
People quietly going back to the old process is feedback about the product, not about the people.
followups: What exactly do you do about the pilot result in the first two weeks?
How do you choose the stores for each wave, and what criteria must a wave meet before the next starts?
Adoption is high but the outcome has not improved in the first wave. What do you look at, and what do you change?
A regional leader asks for a dashboard that shows which associates use the new flow and which do not. What do you say, and what do you offer instead?
In your real example, what did you learn from the people who had to adopt the change, and what did it make you change?

rules.ask: Who sees it, at what level of aggregation, and how do you make sure it is never used to single out individual people?
Stores comply on paper and work around the flow in practice. How would you find out, and what would you change in the product?
Which result in a wave would make you stop the next one, and who agreed to that before it started?
Store teams cannot step away for training before peak. How else does the knowledge reach them, and how do you know it did?
What did you personally decide or do, and when?

templates.title: A central platform team's standards versus many product teams' autonomy
templates.subtopic: platform standards, exceptions, cost of compliance

standard: one event schema registry that every team must publish through
one shared definition of 'in stock' used by every product surface
a common data-quality check suite required before any dataset is published
holdout: the online grocery team, who ship every week and say the process adds days to each change
the store systems team, whose devices cannot run the shared client library
the marketplace team, whose data comes from sellers and does not fit the standard's assumptions

sections.scenario: You lead a central data platform team in a retailer with {{teams}} product teams across stores, e-commerce, fulfilment and pricing. Last year your team introduced {{standard}}. Most teams have adopted it, and incidents caused by inconsistent data have fallen. One team has not: {{holdout}}. Leadership asks you to make the standard mandatory for every team within {{months}} months, and the holdout team's lead has asked for a permanent exception.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you decide which parts of the standard must be mandatory and which can be recommended, how you work with the holdout team, how exceptions are decided and reviewed, what your own team changes, and how you would know whether the standard is worth what it costs the teams that follow it. Then tell me about a real time you set or enforced a technical standard across teams you did not manage, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You do not manage the product teams. Product teams' leads own their roadmaps. The standard's benefits are shared, while its costs fall on each team.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Distinguishes the shared interface (what must be true at the boundary, for example a schema contract or a single metric definition) from implementation freedom; listens to the holdout team and fixes the platform's own friction (faster review paths, a lighter client, adapters for devices or seller data); a written exception process with criteria, an owner, review and expiry; evidence of benefit and cost, including cost to teams; honest counsel to leadership on mandate timing with a plan and evidence; treats other teams' requests consistently; real example with personal contribution and measurable outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is the holdout team's complaint valid?
clarifications.a: Partly. Some of it is real friction your team created; some is preference.

clarifications.q: Who decides exceptions today?
clarifications.a: Nobody formally; your team has granted a few informally.

clarifications.q: What evidence exists for the benefit?
clarifications.a: Incident counts before and after for adopting teams, and some anecdotes. Nobody has measured the cost.

clarifications.q: What happens if the holdout team never adopts?
clarifications.a: Their data feeds several shared reports, which are where most remaining inconsistencies appear.

hints: Separate the interface everyone must meet from how each team meets it.
A standard that costs a team days per change is partly your team's product problem.
An exception process with criteria, an owner and an expiry date is more durable than an informal yes.
followups: Which parts of the standard are truly mandatory, and how did you decide?
What do you change in your own platform to remove the holdout team's legitimate friction?
Leadership wants a mandate; you think a mandate now would backfire. What do you tell them, and with what evidence?
Another team asks for the same exception the holdout team got. How do you decide?
In your real example, what did enforcing the standard cost, and was it worth it?

rules.ask: The holdout team ships weekly. Your gate blocks a fix during peak season. Who can override it, and how fast?
What are the criteria for an exception, who decides, and when does it expire?
What did the holdout team actually tell you, and which part of it did you change your platform for?
How would you measure what the standard costs each team, not only what it saves?
What did you personally do with the holdout team's lead, and when?

templates.title: Leading a team that is half contractors, with different incentives and tenure
templates.subtopic: mixed workforce, knowledge concentration, inclusion within agreed terms

issue: only contractors know how the nightly replenishment jobs work
contractors are not invited to design reviews and have stopped raising problems
employees take the new design work while contractors carry most of the on-call pages
milestone: the move of store inventory feeds to a new platform
the readiness work for the holiday peak
the launch of pickup slot capacity in a new region

sections.scenario: You have just taken over a data engineering team of {{size}} people; half are contractors provided by an outside firm, most on engagements of about a year, and half are employees. In your first weeks you find that {{issue}}. The team must deliver {{milestone}} in {{weeks}} weeks. Two contractors' engagements end shortly after that, and one of them is the person the team calls when something breaks.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover what you do in the first weeks, how you reduce the team's dependence on a few people, how you make the team work as one team within what the contracting agreement allows, how you protect the milestone, and how you handle the engagements that are ending. Then tell me about a real time you led or worked in a team with a mix of employees and contractors, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You cannot change contracts, rates or terms; the outside firm employs its people, and your company has rules about how contractors' work is directed and what they may access. You cannot promise anyone a job. The milestone date is fixed.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical; nothing here describes any company's staffing arrangements.
sections.criteria: Diagnoses knowledge and risk concentration early (who can fix what, which jobs have one expert); treats the team as one in information, design discussion, credit and fair on-call, within the agreement and company rules, asking HR or procurement rather than guessing; plans and verifies knowledge transfer (pairing, rotation, runbooks tested in drills) before engagements end; raises extension or staffing needs early through the right channels without promising outcomes; protects the milestone with an explicit trade-off; addresses employees' attitudes directly and respectfully; real example with personal actions and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Can contractors attend design reviews and on-call?
clarifications.a: Your company allows both, within the agreement; ask HR or procurement if unsure rather than guessing.

clarifications.q: Can the ending engagements be extended?
clarifications.a: Possibly, through procurement and the outside firm; it is not your decision alone.

clarifications.q: Is anything documented?
clarifications.a: Some runbooks exist, out of date. Most knowledge is in people's heads.

clarifications.q: How do the employees feel?
clarifications.a: Some think contractors should just "do the tickets"; others are uneasy with that.

hints: Start by finding where knowledge and risk are concentrated, and in whom.
Treat everyone as part of one team in how work, information and credit are shared, while respecting the agreement's terms.
Knowledge transfer is work: plan it, staff it and check it, especially before an engagement ends.
followups: What do you do in your first two weeks, and what do you not change yet?
How do you transfer the knowledge of the person everyone calls before their engagement ends, without stalling the milestone?
An employee says contractors should not be in design reviews because "they will be gone next year". What do you say?
The milestone and the knowledge transfer compete for the same people in the last three weeks. How do you decide?
In your real example, what did you do to make the team work as one, and what was the result?

rules.ask: Who checks that the runbook works? Has someone other than the author run it during an incident?
You cannot promise that. What do you tell the contractor while procurement decides?
Pairing takes time from the milestone. How much, and how did you decide it was worth it?
How do you make the on-call load fair across the whole team, and what changes for the person who carries most of it now?
What did you personally decide or do, and when?

templates.title: Bringing a vendor-run system in-house before the contract ends
templates.subtopic: discovery, parallel run, cut-over and rollback against a fixed end date

system: the service that turns price changes into store shelf-label and signage data
the service that authorises returns and computes refund amounts
gap: the vendor's documentation covers the API but not the nightly batch jobs behind it
about a third of the business rules exist only as settings in the vendor's console
the vendor will export current data but not history older than two years

sections.scenario: A retailer has run {{system}} on an outside vendor's platform for years. The contract ends in {{months}} months and will not be renewed; leadership has decided to bring the capability in-house, and you lead the work with {{team}}. Stores and online customers depend on the service every day. In discovery you learn that {{gap}}. The vendor is cooperative but has less reason to help as the end date approaches.
sections.problem: How do you lead it? Cover how you find out everything the current system does, including what nobody wrote down; how you decide what to rebuild exactly, what to change and what to drop; how you prove the new system behaves the same where it must; the cut-over and rollback plan; how you manage the vendor relationship through the exit; and what you do if the date is at risk. Then tell me about a real migration off a system you did not build, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The contract end date does not move. Stores cannot tolerate a day without the service. Contract and commercial matters are handled by procurement and legal, not by you.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical; nothing here describes any company's actual vendors, contracts or systems.
sections.criteria: Discovery that treats observed behaviour as the specification (inventory of inputs, outputs, consumers, schedules; console settings and batch jobs captured while access exists; history exported early); scope split into parity, deliberate changes and removals, agreed with consumers, with new features after cut-over unless essential; a parallel run with output comparison at a defined grain and an explained-difference log; staged cut-over by consumer or region with a rehearsed rollback while the vendor system still runs; a constructive vendor relationship with contract matters left to procurement and legal; early, evidence-based decision on extension risk; real example with personal contribution and lessons, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Can the contract be extended for a short period?
clarifications.a: Possibly at a high price; it would need a strong case through procurement.

clarifications.q: Do you have production data from the vendor's system?
clarifications.a: Its outputs and current data, yes; its internal logs, no.

clarifications.q: Who uses the outputs?
clarifications.a: Store systems, the website, finance reports and two other internal teams.

clarifications.q: What did the business ask for beyond parity?
clarifications.a: Two long-requested changes; leadership would like them "if possible".

hints: The system's real specification is its observed behaviour: inputs, outputs and the cases in between. Capture it before the vendor relationship ends.
A parallel run comparing the two systems' outputs on real inputs tells you where you differ and why.
Decide early what would make you ask for an extension, and what it would cost, so the decision is not made in the last week.
followups: What do you do in the first month?
How do you recover the rules that exist only in the vendor's console or batch jobs, and how do you know you found them all?
The parallel run shows 2% of outputs differ. How do you decide which differences matter?
Leadership wants the two new features in the first release. What do you say?
In your real example, what did you discover late, and what would you do earlier next time?

rules.ask: The new system fails two hours after the switch on a busy Saturday. What is the rollback, and has it been rehearsed while the vendor's system still runs?
What exactly do you compare, at what grain, and how many differences are you prepared to accept at cut-over?
Every improvement makes the parallel run harder to read. Which changes ship before cut-over, and which after?
What evidence would justify an extension, who would you take it to, and by when?
What did you personally decide or do, and when?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for omnichannel retail at store scale
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, store-local time, offline sources and reconciliation

angle: the data model and the keys
the hardest failure you diagnosed in it
the decision you would most like to undo
requirement: store numbers that reconcile exactly to each register's end-of-day totals
every report in each store's local business day, including the days clocks change
stores whose data arrives hours late without silently changing numbers people already acted on
customer and associate data visible only in aggregate
scale: thousands of stores, each with its own registers and handheld devices
hundreds of millions of store-item rows refreshed every day
billions of register line items a year

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change for omnichannel retail at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The omnichannel retail setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible re-examination that names the assumptions that would not survive the scale and addresses {{requirement}} incrementally (for example per-register sequence numbers and end-of-day totals reconciled by store and register; a business day computed from each store's time zone at ingestion and stored with the record; versioned, labelled restatement with a changes view rather than silent overwrites; aggregation thresholds and access controls that keep individual customers and associates out of analytics); own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a retail system?
clarifications.a: No. Any system that moved, stored or computed data others depended on; the re-examination is where we bring it into this domain.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to keys, schemas, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.

For the re-examination, start from one record, such as a register line item: where it is created, when it arrives, which store and day it belongs to, and which of its fields the requirement constrains.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Which parts of your design would not survive a scale of {{scale}}? What breaks first?
How would you provide {{requirement}} without a rewrite?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
